title: Molecular systematics and phylogeography of the salt marsh snakes, Nerodia clarkii, using mtDNA d-loop sequences

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620-5150 USA

abstract_text: The salt marsh snake, Nerodia clarkii, is the only North American snake species restricted to brackish water habitats and has evolved unique physiological and behavioral specializations associated with a saline environment. Two of the three subspecies (N. c. compressicauda and N. c. taeniata) are endemic to Florida and are threatened by progressive destruction of coastal wetland habitat. By using the subspecies as the focal taxonomic division in conservation and management programs, we imply that the subspecies is an independent evolutionary lineage worth protecting. As such, the taxonomic status and evolutionary history of subspecies must be ascertained prior to implementing conservation or management programs. Markers used in delineating two of the three subspecies have been vague or highly variable and have failed to consistently differentiate individuals of known identity into their respective taxonomic group. Further, the divergence of the salt marsh snakes from an ancestral freshwater form near the end of the Pliocene has been theorized, but with varying models. We sequenced the mtDNA control region of individuals from the Nerodia clarkii subspecies, Nerodia fasciata subspecies, and several outgroup taxa in order to elucidate the relationship among the salt marsh snakes and to better understand the evolutionary history of the group.

abstract_text: Five hundred seventy two Sceloporus occidentalis from two nearby populations in Los Angeles County, California were examined for helminths: 200 from the San Gabriel Mountains (montane ca. 1584 m elevation) and 372 from the Puente Hills, Whittier (lowland ca. 150 m elevation). The component helminth community of the montane fence lizard population consisted of four species: two species of cestodes, Mesocestoides sp. and Oochoristica scelopori and two species of nematodes, Physaloptera retusa and Spauligodon giganticus. The component helminth community of the lowland fence lizard population contained three species: Mesocestoides sp., Physaloptera retusa and unidentified acuariid larvae. The two helminth communities were dissimilar in composition. Each host population must be examined; helminth community composition cannot be assumed.

title: Trematode parasitism of the Canadian red-sided garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis): A study in prevalence and intensity

abstract_text: One-hundred and ninety-four Canadian red-sided garter snakes were collected from the Interlake region north of Winnipeg, Manitoba, over a two year period, in the spring and fall seasons of 1996 and 1997. This snake is host to a lung inhabiting digenetic trematode of the family Plagiorchiidae. The infection is acquired by the consumption of tadpoles and frogs. These intermediate hosts harbor the metacercarial cysts that may further develop into mature, egg producing adults, when consumed. It has been reported that the minimum time requirement for the appearance of an adult trematode in the lung is greater than eight weeks. All snakes examined for trematode infection were preserved, measured for length, and gender determined. The adult trematodes were counted and removed, with their locations being recorded. The data were used to evaluate the prevalence (percent rate of infection) and intensity (number of parasites per host). The prevalence of the trematode infection was higher in females (35%) than in males (15%). The mean intensity was also higher in females (10+2, range: 1-65) than in males (5+1, range: 1-13). No significant correlation between intensity and snout-vent length was found in either sex. However, there is evidence to suggest that prevalence increases with snout-vent length. A group of long term captive (> 12 weeks) snakes were compared to the sample of wild snakes. There were no significant differences in the mean intensities of the wild and long-term captive animals. However, the prevalence in the females increased from 35% to 53% and increased in males from 15% to 30%.

title: The influence of moonlight, temperature, hydrostatic pressure and zooplankton abundance upon the vertical distribution and relative abundance of mesopelagic fishes in the epipelagic zone at night

abstract_text: Four cruises, with a 4-m2 Multiple Opening/Closing Net and Environmental Sensing System (MOCNESS), were conducted to investigate the influence of moonlight, temperature, hydrostatic pressure and zooplankton abundance upon the nighttime vertical distribution and relative abundance of mesopelagic micronekton in the epipelagic zone of the eastern Gulf of Mexico. Two hundred and fifteen trawl hauls, sampling discrete 25-meter depth strata between the surface and 175 meters, were completed. Environmental parameters (temperature, hydrostatic pressure and moon phase) and zooplankton abundance were recorded for each trawl haul. Additionally, measurements of the nighttime light field and diffuse attenuation coefficient were recorded during two 1989 cruises. Vertical distributions for the abundant fish species tended to be shallower during new moon phases. Two statistical methods (Canonical Correspondence Analysis and Analysis of Covariance) indicated that hydrostatic pressure, temperature and moon phase influenced the relative abundances of fishes and that light at depth was especially important in influencing relative abundances during the 1989 cruises. Despite the importance of light at depth, the abundant species were not limited to specific levels of ambient light.

title: Effect of light on juvenile walleye pollock shoaling and their interaction with predators

authors.affiliation: Alaska Fisheries Science Center, NMFS, NOAA, Hatfield Marine Science Center, Newport, Oregon 97365 USA

abstract_text: Under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark photoperiod, juvenile walleye pollock displayed a diurnal schooling and activity pattern, characterized by cohesive shoaling during the day, with a cessation of shoaling and decreased swimming speeds at night. Juvenile walleye pollock were not characterized by a distinct light threshold for shoaling; shoals gradually dispersed as light levels decreased and gradually recoalesced as light levels increased. At light levels below 2.8x10-9 mEs-1m-2 juvenile walleye pollock were so dispersed as to no longer constitute a shoal. Exposure to simulated predation had differing effects upon fish behavior under light and dark conditions. Brief exposure to a model predator in the dark, caused fish to swim faster than fish which had been exposed in the light. Chronic exposure to a living predator produced similar results; fish tended to swim slower when a predator was present in the light, but faster when a predator was present in the dark. In the light, predation can result in cohesive shoals, but in the dark, increased activity may accelerate shoal dispersal, suggesting that perceived predation risk has opposite effects upon the spatial distribution of shoaling fish under light and dark conditions.

title: Prey-type effect on raking behavior in the osteoglossomorph fish Chitala chitala

abstract_text: Fishes of the subdivision Osteoglossomorpha ("bony tongues") possess a functional novelty the "tongue-bite apparatus," located between the mandibular jaw apparatus anteriorly and the pharyngeal jaw apparatus posteriorly. Previous work on this group described a distinct behavior known as "raking" associated with this novel feeding mechanism. Using high-speed video (250 fields s-1) and stop-frame kinematic analysis, raking behavior for two prey types (earthworms and goldfish) was characterized in the clown knifefish (Chitala chitala). Kinematic data will be presented that reveals raking is a modulated behavior.

title: Feeding ecology, activity patterns and spatial distribution of Siluriformes in a stream of Atlantic rainforest in south-eastern Brazil

abstract_text: The Atlantic rainforest ichthyofauna is rich in siluriforms, with many endemic species. Seventy percent of the species recorded in the Betari stream, Upper Ribeira Valley, Eastern Brazilian basin, are siluriforms belonging to the following families: Loricariidae (eight species), Pimelodidae (four species), Trichomycteridae (two species) and Callichthyidae (one species). Between June 1996 and February 1998, I studied spatial distribution, activity patterns, and feeding ecology of these fishes in a stream section one kilometer long. Diurnal and nocturnal transects were made at different sites using snorkelling. Half of the studied species are distributed in patches, with water current, depth and type of substrate influencing their distribution patterns. Except for Otocinclus gibbosus (Loricariidae) and Trichomycterus davisi (Trichomycteridae) all other siluriforms studied are nocturnal. The loricariids graze on algae covering rock, mostly diatoms, organic detritus and sediment. Corydoras barbatus (Callichthyidae) feeds on aquatic insects and algae. The pimelodids are generalists carnivores, with Rhamdia quelen preying on fish and crustaceans, and Rhamdioglanis frenatus preying on aquatic invertebrates, especially insects (Trichoptera). This study is a contribution to the knowledge on the poorly known ichthyofauna from the Atlantic rainforest.

title: Diet overlap and resource use by five species of butterflyfish (Family Chaetodontidae) in Fiji

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, SUNY at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY 14260 USA
Department of Natural Sciences, Long Island University, NY 11968 USA

abstract_text: We investigated the applicability of five species of butterflyfish as biological indicators on the Great Astrolabe Reef, Fiji. Availability and patterns of resource use by the butterflyfish were investigated. Individuals of 3-13 pairs of each species were followed and feeding rates and foraging areas were recorded. For four of the five species of butterflyfish, acroporid corals constituted the dominant food in the diet. Chaetodon pelewensis and C. citrinellus were not obligate corallivores, feeding upon coralline algae and filamentous algae. The remaining species were obligate corallivores. Chaetodon trifascialis and C. baronessa showed a preference for acroporid corals and can be considered feeding specialists. Chaetodon trifasciatus is a feeding generalist, with no clear preference for any of a wide variety of corals in the diet. Among specialists and generalists diet overlap was high, but between specialists and generalists there was less diet overlap. In addition, foraging areas of the different species overlapped, in some cases almost 100%, suggesting that food resources are being shared.

title: Influences of an exotic cordgrass on estuarine fish diets in Willapa Bay, WA

authors.affiliation: Ohio Cooperative Fish & Wildlife Research Unit, Department of Zoology, The Ohio State University, 1735 Neil Ave., Columbus OH 43210 USA

abstract_text: Invasions of introduced species as a result of human activities have had huge impacts on aquatic ecosystems. Furthermore, introduced species may become permanent components of these ecosystems. As a consequence it becomes important for scientists and managers to understand the physical and biological processes within these rapidly changing environments. We examined the effects of Spartina alterniflora invasion within an estuary along the Washington coast. Between April and September in 1994 & 1995, we sampled fishes over mudflats and within differently sized Spartina clones (3m, 6m, 12m, and meadows). Distribution and abundance of native fishes varied both temporally and spatially as a consequence of the presence or absence of Spartina, as clones grew seasonally and as different fishes recruited to the area. Cymatogaster, Leptocottus, and Oncorhynchus diets failed to correspond to habitat use differences. Instead, their diets reflected a mix of prey derived from mudflat and Spartina-inhabited areas. In addition to a prey mix reflective of habitats, fishes consumed large proportions of exotic prey species (i.e., cumaceans, amphipods). The invasion of exotic species to this estuary probably proceeded along several paths, however, the impact of aquaculture practices and culturing of a non-native oyster species most likely had the greatest influence.

title: The relationship between the threespine stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus, and the cestode parasite Schistocephalus solidus in Walby Lake, Alaska; new perspectives of the host-parasite system

abstract_text: The threespine stickleback is an intermediate host of the cestode Schistocephalus solidus. Prior research has led to the hypothesis that selection has resulted in a delay of the deleterious effects of Schistocephalus on stickleback until after stickleback complete reproduction. Other research has concluded that any heavily infected female stickleback are unlikely to spawn because Schistocephalus delays or inhibits ovarian maturation. The intensity, prevalence, and severity of infection of stickleback from Walby Lake, Alaska, are inconsistent with the results of previous investigations, showing that reproduction and high levels of infection may occur. Our data suggest there may be previously unobserved adverse effects of parasitism on clutch parameters in parasitized stickleback females. We will discuss possible reasons for the differences we have observed for Walby Lake after contrasting our results with those of previous studies.

title: Population ecology of Rhamdioglanis frenatus and Pimelodella transitoria (Siluriformes: Pimelodidae) in a stream from the atlantic rainforest, south-eastern Brazil

abstract_text: Population ecology of Rhamdioglanis frenatus and Pimelodella transitoria from the Betari river, Upper Ribeira Valley, State of Sao Paulo, was studied by the mark-recapture method between Mar. 1987 and Feb. 1998. After eleven monthly collections, 171 specimens of R. frenatus and 104 of P. transitoria longer than 80 mm SL were marked by tattooing in a 2.000 m section of the river. Preliminary estimates indicate populations sizes of 300-500 individuals for R. frenatus and 800-2500 for P. transitoria, with populations densities varying between 0.01-0.02 and 0.04-0.12 individuals m-2 respectively. These catfishes are sedentary, being recaptured at the same site of previous collections at rates as high as 85% for R. frenatus and 95% for P. transitoria. Upstream and downstream movements were recorded, without clear tendencies. Individual growth rates for R. frenatus and P. transitoria were 0.2 cm month-1 and less than 0.1 cm month-1, respectively, but preliminary data indicate those rates may double in the rainy season. Microhabitat distribution data obtained from captures indicate preference for pools and low migration rates between pools in both species. Rhamdioglanis frenatus is solitary, while P. transitoria is gregarious, specially during daytime.

title: The role of transient predators in regulating juvenile reef fish abundance on small patch reefs: a preliminary examination

abstract_text: As part of an ongoing research program designed to investigate local reef fish recruitment processes, the importance of post-settlement predation was examined. A series of recently completed experiments manipulated prey refugia and resident fish abundance on small (1 m3) model patch reefs. Although these experiments were not designed to determine the relative importance of resident versus transient predators, a portion of the data obtained, as well as ancillary observations, support the hypothesis that transient predators (e.g. Carangids) have an important role in regulating juvenile reef fish abundance. At the very least, our results indicate that specific studies are required to elucidate the influence of transient predators on small patch reef fish assemblages. The aim of this presentation is to stimulate further discussion on the processes that regulate reef fish assemblages.

abstract_text: Fish assemblages in 14 individual pools within a 1-km reach of Brier Creek, Oklahoma, were censused by snorkeling on 17 dates from 1982 to 1997, with intervals between surveys ranging from 2 weeks to 11 years. During our period of sampling some intervals included major floods or drought, whereas other intervals were 'benign'. title: Aquatic, terrestrial and "global" landscape factors: which most influence local stream fish assemblages?

authors.affiliation: Museum of Natural History and Biological Survey, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73019 USA
Department of Zoology and Biological Station, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73019 USA

abstract_text: Stream fish ecology offers conflicting hypotheses about environmental and landscape factors controlling local assemblage structure, at scales from local "microhabitat" to "global" or macroecological. Using a large, time-delimited data base, spanning a wide range of local settings in midwestern North America, we tested suites of physical or landscape factors as predictors of structure or emergent properties of local fish assemblages, at scales including: (1) "within reach" (aquatic); (2) local area (terrestrial); and (3) within basin, and (4) among named river basins. In June-July 1995, we sampled stream fishes at 65 sites spanning 1700 km across Iowa, Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas. At each site all apparent microhabitats were sampled, and environmental or landscape variables were documented. "Global" factors (rainfall, meteorological) were obtained from standard references. Basin identity explained much variation in composition of local fish assemblages as reflected by scores of "sites" in a DCA based on abundance. In a PCA including all environmental/landscape variables, latitude (a surrogate for "basin identity") was related strongly to fish assemblage composition. On the other hand, emergent properties of assemblages (e.g., richness) were not influenced by basin or latitude. Subsequent PCAs, based separately on within-reach "aquatic" and local area "terrestrial" factors showed that landscape within the stream (depth, current, presence of gravel patches) influenced species richness more than extrinsic terrestrial factors.

title: The estuarine Artenminimum: evidence from the lower Chesapeake Bay

authors.affiliation: College of William & Mary, School of Marine Science, P.O. Box 1346, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA

abstract_text: The dramatic biological, chemical, and physical changes in the low salinity habitats of estuaries are thought to limit the number of resident faunal taxa. Remane (1934) first described this phenomena, a species minimum occurring near oligohaline salinities (5-8 ppt), from invertebrate assemblages of large stable brackish lakes. It has since been proffered as a general feature of the estuarine gradient, though examples from the primary literature are rare. Two possible complications to the location of this pattern in estuarine fishes are: (1) the large number of seasonal migratory species who exhibit changing salinity preferences with ontogeny; and, (2) the failure to standardize species richness estimates to a measure of sample size (i.e., rarefaction). I applied rarefaction techniques to seine and trawl survey data to investigate whether this phenomena is evident in fish assemblages from three tributaries of the lower Chesapeake Bay. Results of the analysis indicate a minimum can occur, and is most evident in systems with a physically long salinity gradient. Beta diversity calculations confirmed the region of highest species turnover was displaced upstream from the minimum (near 0-2 ppt), and coincides with the most severe changes in ionic ratios. Hence, distance to source pools of marine and freshwater taxa appears to interact with salinity preferences to establish the minimum. Excursions from most favorable habitats by a highly mobile species appears spatially similar to recruitment survival in sessile invertebrates, and may explain the similarity in pattern between the two groups.

title: Reproduction and early ontogeny of the sand diver, Trichonotus setiger, from Papua New Guinea

abstract_text: Observation Point at the northwest end of Normanby Island (Milne Bay Province) is the home of a taxocene with four to five species of sand divers, Trichonotus, one of them the recently described T. halstead. In 1997 and 1998 we returned to study their early life history. Purported gill-chamber brooding was not confirmed by dissections of many specimens. The sympatric species live in distinct harem territories or swarms on a sandy slope where they mate soon after sunrise. T. setiger, mating over coarse sand, deposit many small eggs. Mature females (~ 8.7 cm TL) had ovaries with 150 to 200 oocytes. When mating is over, eggs were scooped up with sand from the mating site, rushed into the boat, and observed live under special microscopes. Deposited translucent eggs (0.6 mm) stick to the sand grains. The clear yolk contains one large yellowish oil globule. Development was observed at 25-26 C: after 30 min, four cells had formed. Ten hours later, heart beat and blood circulation could be seen. Hatching occurred 13-13.5 hours after spawning. The just hatched embryos (ca. 2.2 mm TL, >38 somites) were translucent with completely unpigmented eyes. Initially the embryos were mostly resting at the bottom, occasionally wriggling, later darting around and into the water column. When motionless, they slowly sank head first. At 18 h a white pigment was observed around the anus, later white pigment accumulated around the notochord towards the tip of the tail, and finally in the head region. When one day old (3 mm TL) the yolksac had decreased in size; initially, the oil globule was about 1/4 of the yolksac length, now it took 1/3 of yolk size. At age two days the embryos had reached a TL of 4.5 mm. The snout region had become more pointed but neither jaw movements nor gut contents were observed, i.e. exogenous feeding was not yet started. These findings will be discussed with respect to the distribution of the sand divers and a possible direct development without a planktonic larva, a rare thing in coral reef fishes.

abstract_text: Food habits data collected on Northeast Fisheries Science Center groundfish surveys between Nova Scotia and Cape Fear from 1981-1990 were analyzed to categorize abundant species into feeding types (e.g., piscivorus, molluscivorus, etc.), and to examine changes in feeding types through ontogeny. Over 83,000 stomach samples from 51 species (13 elasmobranch, 36 teleost, and 2 cephalopod species) were included in the analysis. Predator feeding types representing primary reliance on Annelida (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus, Pleuronectes americanus and Pleuronectes ferrugineus), Arthropoda (9 species including 4 > 80%: Sebastes fasciatus, Scomber scombrus, Raja senta, and Mustelus canis), Mollusca (Myliobatis freminvillei and Merluccius albidus), Echinodermata (Hippoglossoides platessoides), and Fish (17 species including 4 > 90%: Pomatomus saltatrix, Carcharhinus plumbeus, Synodus foetens, and Lophius americanus) were found. title: The influence of riparian buffer strips on fishes: are we measuring the right things?

authors.affiliation: Institute of Ecology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602 USA

abstract_text: Discussions of the influence of riparian vegetation on stream health focus on the width of such buffer zones. Policy decisions and environmental regulations similarly use riparian width as the metric of importance. We sampled fishes and stream habitats in 12 stream segments downstream from deforested riparian patches 0 - 5.6 km long, all downslope from densely forested watersheds. We found that the strongest predictors of fish abundance and occurrence were area and particularly length of the riparian patch; patch width was a relatively poor predictor of fish occurrence. Limited riparian clearing may cause minor disturbance to the fish assemblage, but streams in even a heavily forested watershed cannot tolerate disruption of the riparian zone of much more than 1 km in length. Riparian buffer length should be given stronger consideration in stream protection and restoration plans.

title: Sensory mechanisms underpinning feeding behavior in elasmobranchs

authors.affiliation: School of Biological Sciences, University of Auckland

abstract_text: Elasmobranchs have some sophisticated feeding strategies, ranging from tail clipping bill-fishes, to locating concentrations of patchily distributed prey. These strategies are underpinned by an equally sophisticated array of sensory systems. To take one example, many rays feed on buried bivalves, and dig where the prey densities are high (Hine et al. 1997). Behavioral studies (Montgomery and Skipworth, 1997) illustrate the potential importance of mechanosensory systems in this feeding behavior. Both mechanosensory and electrosensory systems share a high level of sensitivity, to the extent that behaviorally relevant inputs could be swamped by self-generated noise. One interesting aspect of the sensory biology of elasmobranchs is that hindbrain signal processing effectively resolves this problem (Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994).

title: Selective foraging behaviour of basking sharks on zooplankton in tidal fronts

abstract_text: Individual and grouped basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus) filter-feeding on zooplankton at the water's surface were tracked visually together with zooplankton sampling from their feeding paths. Along tidal slicks they exhibited area-restricted searching behaviour and actively selected areas containing high densities of large zooplankton above a threshold level. Basking sharks remained in the most profitable patches transported by tidal currents for up to 27h and moved between patches over 24-48h periods. Between years, the location of shark foraging areas changed according to the effects of prevailing weather conditions on frontal boundary sharpness and the maintenance of frontal upwellings. Our results show that basking sharks are selective filter-feeders on specific zooplankton assemblages and therefore useful as biological indicators of abundance trends in zooplankton species influenced by climatic fluctuations of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO).

title: Evolutionary innovations in the feeding mechanism of elasmobranchs

authors.affiliation: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697 USA

abstract_text: A major conclusion from comparative studies of feeding mechanisms in lower vertebrates is that some of the biomechanical couplings involved in mouth opening have been retained throughout evolution. However, recent studies of the jaw mechanism indicate that elasmobranchs differ from other lower vertebrates in that the geniohyoideus coupling is the primary mechanism for lower jaw depression rather than the rectus cervicus coupling. In addition, previous studies of the feeding mechanism in lower vertebrates indicate that structural differences among taxa may arise by the addition of a novel structure or as a result of modification of the existing musculoskeletal apparatus. Accompanying such changes, the ancestral motor pattern may be retained or the timing of motor activity may be altered. Evolutionary innovations in the musculoskeletal apparatus mediating upper jaw protrusion in elasmobranchs has involved both the addition of a novel feature, the dorsal preorbitalis coupling, and by the modification of an existing structure, the levator palatoquadrati coupling, while retaining the ancestral system, the ventral preorbitalis coupling. These changes in the musculoskeletal apparatus have involved conservation of the motor pattern in the ancestral mechanism and alteration of the motor pattern in the modified mechanism.

title: Suction feeding in sharks: a kinematic analysis of feeding in the nurse shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum

authors.affiliation: University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida, 33620 USA

abstract_text: Despite relatively simple feeding mechanisms, sharks exhibit a variety of feeding types. Ancestral cladodont sharks presumably grasped and possibly swallowed their prey whole. Modern sharks have radiated to include biting, gouging and biting, ram-feeding, suction-feeding, filter-feeding, and crushing types. Convergence and specialization for suction feeding have arisen in a variety of divergent extant taxa. The orectolobiform nurse shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum, is a specialized and apparently obligate suction feeder. Kinematic analysis from high speed video of five sharks reveals a conservative feeding sequence involving mandible depression and labial cartilage protrusion, followed by mandible elevation and labial cartilage retraction. The expansive and compressive phases are very rapid, with a mean duration of 92 ms. Similar to other elasmobranchs, there is significant variability among sharks in nine kinematic variables. Within sharks, bite durations are very constant as the sharks become satiated. The suction feeding nurse shark differs from ram feeding carcharhinid sharks by its short and relatively constant durations of mouth expansion, minimal contribution of palatoquadrate protrusion and cranial elevation, reduced dentition, formation of a laterally enclosed and anteriorly directed mouth, and hypertrophied abductor muscles. Continuing studies seek functional and evolutionary patterns in shark feeding.

title: Mechanics and modulation of prey capture in generalists vs. specialist predators: a kinematic comparison using two carcharhiniform sharks

authors.affiliation: University of California, Irvine, CA 92697-2525 USA

abstract_text: Recent work on teleosts suggests that attack kinematics (= behaviors) may be modified by a predator based on specific attributes of the prey item. Sharks are generally presumed to be highly visual predators and, thus, it is reasonable to expect that they are also capable of such modulation. Work on swellsharks, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, however, indicated that prey size did not induce modulation. To determine the generality of this finding, I investigated the effect of both prey size and elusivity on prey capture kinematics in a species with a more generalized diet, the leopard shark, Triakis semifasciata. Sharks were filmed using high speed video feeding on two sizes of the same prey (shrimp pieces) and two more elusive prey (earthworms and live mud shrimp). In leopard sharks, size effects were noted for kinematic parameters related to buccal cavity expansion. Elusivity effects were not detected for any parameters, but a performance consequence was also not detected with increasingly elusive prey. These studies cumulatively suggest that rather than possessing a single attack behavior, generalists are capable of kinematic modulation. They also suggest that the phrase 'master of none' that is typically used to describe a 'jack of all trades' generalist may not apply.

title: A review of South African feeding studies of elasmobranch fishes: Perspectives and future directions

authors.affiliation: Port Elizabeth Museum, P.O. Box 13147, Humewood, 6013, South Africa

abstract_text: A review of the South African literature over the last decade shows that more than 20 papers have been published dealing with elasmobranch feeding, although many were part of general studies of their biology. They describe the feeding of more than 50 elasmobranch species based on identification of recently ingested prey. Accurate prey identification was possible in many studies using digestion-resistant prey hard parts such as cephalopod beaks and fish otoliths, which allowed more precise understanding of the impact of each species. The relationship between predator size and prey choice is crucial but was often not described. Although such studies provide insights into prey taken, on their own they are poor reflections of the complex interactions between predator and prey over time. Studies of predator/prey interactions in the wild have been initiated and such studies are vital to clearer understanding of predation. The large size of most chondrichthyans limits their suitability in laboratory based experimental studies, but the rapid advances in the technology of electronic tracking devices is facilitating remote data collection in the wild, thereby augmenting direct observations. This promising area of research has the potential to clarify details of behaviour and feeding ecology that otherwise would be unobtainable.

title: Dietary changes associated with life history and sex for the sevengill shark: Implications for intraspecific competition and resource partitioning

authors.affiliation: US Abalone, P.O. Box 254, Davenport, CA 95017, USA

abstract_text: Dietary changes associated with life history stage and sex for the sevengill shark are analysized and discussed. Data collected over a 15 year period were used to analyze the sevengill shark's dietary habits. The size categories were grouped so as to approximate this shark's life history stage; juvenile, adolescent, and adult. In addition, the diet of male and female sharks of each life history stage was compared to note any differences between the sexes. Dietary changes associated with an elasmobranchs life history and sexual stage of development may explain how food resources within a given territory are partitioned such that competition between conspecifics at different stages of life may be reduced. A reduction in competition between conspecifics may have evolved to ensure that resource partitioning and cannibalism would be reduced between conspecifics at different stages of life. Thus increasing survivorship for the species during the critical early stages of life. The implications of dietary changes as related to life history and sexual stage of development may be complex and far reaching, yet may play a critical role in the success of elasmobranchs as a group.

title: The feeding ecology of elasmobranch fishes from the British Isles

authors.affiliation: CEFAS Fisheries Laboratory, Pakefield Road, Lowestoft, Suffolk, NR33 OHT, U.K.
CEFAS Fisheries Laboratory, Pakefield Road, Lowestoft, Suffolk, NR33 OHT, U.K.

abstract_text: The diets of inshore elasmobranchs from the waters of the British Isles are reviewed from historical and contemporary data. The feeding habits of ten of these species (Scyliorhinus canicula, Scyliorhinus stellaris, Mustelus asterias, Galeorhinus galeus, Squatina squatina, Raja brachyura, R. clavata, R. microocellata, R. montagui and R. naevus) are discussed in relation to their comparative feeding ecology, their distributions in the Irish Sea and English Channel, the demersal faunal assemblages to which they belong and their dentition.

title: Tapeworms as indicators of elasmobranch feeding biology

authors.affiliation: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA

abstract_text: Tapeworms are potentially valuable indicators of elasmobranch feeding biology because their life cycles require more than one host species and transmission between these host species is accomplished through predation. Thus, tapeworms enter their elasmobranch hosts when the intermediate hosts in which they reside as larvae are consumed by elasmobranchs. The lack of life cycle data and lack of information on degree of specificity for their final intermediate hosts currently limits the specific predictive value of tapeworms. However, some generalizations can be made from the complete tapeworm assemblage observed in a host. Inconsistencies in the tapeworm assemblages of related elasmobranch species can provide indirect evidence of differences in food habit. For example, the tapeworms of megamouth are fully consistent with this shark's status as a filter feeder rather than an apex predator. Changes in the tapeworm fauna of a host species over time may reflect age related changes in diet. For example, the differences in the tapeworm fauna between small and large individuals of the Atlantic nurse shark may be indicative of a shift in food habit. Depending on their specificity for their intermediate hosts, tapeworms may act as indicators of specific prey species consumed by a host species or individuals.

title: Standardized diet compositions and trophic levels of sharks

authors.affiliation: Institute for Fishery Resource Ecology, National Marine Fisheries Service/Florida State University, 3500 Delwood Beach Road, Panama City, FL 32408, USA

abstract_text: Sharks are marine consumers believed to occupy top positions in marine food webs. But surprisingly few quantitative estimates of trophic levels (TL) exist for this group. With the hope to better define the ecological role of sharks in marine communities, this paper presents standardized diet compositions and trophic levels for a suite of species. Dietary compositions were calculated from published quantitative studies using a weighted average index. TL values of the eleven food types used to characterize the diet were obtained from published accounts and used to calculate fractional trophic levels for 151 species representing seven orders and 21 families. Sharks as a group are tertiary consumers (TL>4), and significant differences were found among six orders compared, attributable mainly to differences between orectolobiformes and all other orders. Among four families of carcharhiniform sharks, carcharhinids had significantly higher TL than triakids and scyliorhinids, but not sphyrnids. When compared to TL for other top predators of marine communities obtained from the literature, mean TL for sharks was significantly higher than for seabirds, but not for marine mammals. Trophic level and body size were positively correlated, with the fit increasing when the three predominantly planktivorous species were omitted and when considering carcharhinids only.

title: Review of rate of consumption, food transit and digestive efficiency in sharks

authors.affiliation: Zoology Department, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, HI, USA

abstract_text: Sharks are important apex consumers in the marine environment and quantification of energy flow through sharks is important for understanding their impact in marine ecosystems. However, there have been relatively few studies on rates of consumption (daily ration) in sharks and it is difficult to generalize about the role of sharks in the flow of energy in an ecosystem. Estimates of the daily ration of sharks generally either incorporate data on the duration and rate of food emptying from the stomach and field observations on prey items ingested, or involve bioenergetic models based on a balanced energy budget. Several factors that may influence rates of consumption are poorly understood in elasmobranchs. There have been few studies on the efficiency of food digestion, absorption and conversion to growth, and the passage of food through the digestive tract, despite the importance of these factors on energy flow through the trophic level occupied by sharks. This study reviews the current state of knowledge on rates of consumption, rates of food transit through the stomach and entire digestive tract, and the efficiency with which ingested food is converted to energy stored as growth in sharks.

title: Feeding habits of the spiny dogfish in British Columbia waters
abstract_text: The Spiny dogfish is the most abundant shark in B.C. waters with biomass estimated to be approximately 200,000 t. Frequenting all depths within coastal shelf and slope habitats, the dogfish is a significant predator within NE Pacific ecosystems impacting a wide variety of vertebrate and invertebrate taxonomic groups spanning several trophic levels. In this paper we summarize the feeding habits of the spiny dogfish in B.C. waters analyzing several data sets collected during the 1970's and 1980's, and comparing them to published literature. In particular, we examine the spatial and temporal variability in dogfish feeding habits and discuss the importance of recognizing bias when attempting to estimate consumption rates of dogfish prey.

title: Captive feeding biology of elasmobranchs

authors.affiliation: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 886 Cannery Row, Monterey, CA 93940, USA

abstract_text: We observed large food consumption of 7.1 (s.e. 0.7, n = 17) percent body-mass per day for a captive juvenile pelagic stingray Dasyatis violacea (disc width 44.4 cm, PIT tag # AVID 017-085-067), in a holding pool kept at 20 C. This confirmed earlier results in the 4600 m3 Outer Bay Water Exhibit of the Monterey Bay Aquarium when 3 juvenile pelagic stingrays were displayed for three months. It suggests possible large differences in food consumption and corresponding growth rates between captive and wild pelagic stingrays. Food consumption and growth rates of juvenile elasmobranchs in captivity are compared with those in the wild. The dietary requirements of captive temperate water sharks in a semi-open sea water system and pelagic stingrays in a nearly closed system are compared with results for elasmobranchs in other aquaria.

title: Bioenergetics models for estimating food consumption in elasmobranch fishes
abstract_text: Measuring food consumption in elasmobranch fishes has proven to be a challenge, and has resulted in the use of a variety of methods. In recent years, bioenergetics models have increased in popularity and complexity. These models take into account energetic costs of living (metabolism, wastes, and growth) in order to estimate consumption requirements. Bioenergetics models have been used to estimate consumption rates for a number of different species including lemon, sandbar, greyreef, galapagos, tiger, bull, spiny dogfish, scalloped hammerhead sharks, and spiny butterfly ray. Like all models, output is reliant on the quality of input data, thus direct measurements of the costs of living and how costs vary with environmental variables and body size are needed. A complete model has been assembled for the lemon shark, which through laboratory and field research has shown good cross-validation. However, accuracy of some models may be questionable due to inclusion of data from other species or by using laboratory data alone. Recent advances in telemetry techniques and captive husbandry may offer new opportunities for estimating energetic parameters in both the field and laboratory. Bioenergetics models may also be useful in quantifying the ecological association of elasmobranchs on habitats and prey populations.

title: Communication signals and endocrine state as mutually interacting systems in anuran amphibians
abstract_text: Much of the communication behavior of anuran amphibians and other vertebrates takes place in the context of reproduction. Many aspects of communication are dependent on, influenced by, hormones associated with reproductive state. Less clearly appreciated is the fact that communication signals influence hormonal state in a variety of vertebrates. Communication and endocrine state should therefore be considered mutually interacting systems. We have used anuran amphibians as a model for investigating this interaction. Our results indicate that the frog auditory system (carrying information about vocal communication signals) connects with several areas of the basal forebrain. Some of these areas contain gonadotropin releasing hormone cells while others contain populations of catecholamine neurons. The latter populations are sensitive to circulating sex steroid hormones, and may be involved in some aspect of reproductive endocrinology or behavior. The strong connections between auditory and endocrine systems in frogs suggest that the reception of communication signals may influence gonadal state. Experiments exposing frogs to conspecific calls support this. Males exposed to conspecific calls showed larger testes and changes in testes histology compared to control animals. In frogs, therefore, vocal communication signals trigger changes in reproductive physiology as well as reproductive behavior.

title: The use of interactive playback and call monitoring to study acoustical interactions in frogs

authors.affiliation: Division of Biological Sciences, Tucker Hall, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO 65211 USA

abstract_text: Male anurans of many species advertise for mates vocally in dense aggregations where they may also interact aggressively with competitors. Recently, sophisticated experimental techniques have been used to address questions about the proximate and ultimate bases of vocal behavior of these animals. For example, with interactive playback an analog or computer-based call synthesizer is made to respond to a calling male after user-specified time delays. I will discuss how I have used this methodology in work on call timing and aggressive behavior. Our understanding of the calling dynamics of chorus members has also benefited from the use of multi-channel equipment to monitor the vocal behavior of two or more males. By using such a system in my studies of Hyla microcephala in Panama, I have found that males respond primarily to their nearest neighbors in the chorus. These results agree with recent findings on acoustically signaling insects. The behavior of males minimizes signal overlap with individuals whose calls are most likely to seriously impair their ability to attract a female. I will also discuss data on vocal interactions among male H. versicolor obtained in an artificial pond where my colleagues and I have manipulated chorus density.

title: Vocal communication and reproductive interactions in Xenopus laevis
abstract_text: Xenopus laevis is a nocturnal Pipid whose native habitat is the murky ponds of South Africa. Two vocal behaviors had been characterized: the advertisement call of sexually receptive males and the release call (ticking) of sexually unreceptive females. We have recently described an additional vocal signal, a fertility advertisement called rapping, given by females just prior to oviposition. Rapping is an acoustic aphrodisiac that stimulates male calling and phonotaxis. Field and laboratory observations suggest that calling is confined to only one or two males at any one time, even in densely populated ponds. We have recorded several male/male vocalizations (e.g. chirping and growling) that might serve to establish male vocal hierarchies at the onset of the breeding season. I will discuss the significance of these calls in reproductive interactions and the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to the sexually differentiated vocal repertoire.

title: Communication and mating in the midwife toads (Alytes obstetricans and Alytes cisternasii). Ten years of studies

authors.affiliation: Centro de Biologia Ambiental, Faculdade de Ciências, Universidade de Lisboa, P 1700 Lisboa, Portugal; Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales, José Gutiérrez Abascal 2, 28006 Madrid, Spain
Dept. of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin TX 78712, USA

abstract_text: Midwife toads are a primitive group of anurans with parental care and highly simplified vocal communication. Several populations of Alytes have been studied in continental Spain since 1987. The distributions of call characteristics overlapped between different population and species. The covariance between temperature and call duration varied between populations of different taxonomic groups. Large male reproductive advantage was found. Phonotaxis tests showed that calls with lower frequencies (emitted by larger males) were more attractive to females than calls with high frequencies. In syntopic populations of the two species there was no sign of character displacement in the male calls, but female preference was different than in allopatric situations. Males increase their calling rate when exposed to a nearby competitor. The response is different according to competitor's size and competitor's calling rate. Call alternation between males is non-random. Although call overlap affects negatively female preference, call alternation does not decrease call overlap. Many of the differences observed in acoustical competition can be related with the differences in mating season length between species, and with the differences in selective pressures that these two scenarios incorporate (male acoustical competition, and female choice based in both dynamic and static call characteristics).

title: Evolutionary aspects of mating call variation in the diploid-tetraploid complex of Bufo viridis

authors.affiliation: Dipartimento di Biologia Animale, Universita di Torino, Via Accademia Albertina, 17, 10123 Torino, Italy
Dipartimento di Biologia Animale, Universita di Torino, Via Accademia Albertina, 17, 10123 Torino, Italy

abstract_text: The asian green toads have been profitably employed as a model for the study of the evolution of vocalizations by comparing diploid, triploid and tetraploid green toads on the basis of morphometrical and acoustical parameters. Since in green toads advertisement calls produced by males play an important role in mate choice, particular attention is given to their differences. Diploid toads show significantly larger body size and proportionally larger head and shorter limbs than both tetraploids and triploids, whereas no evident morphometrical differences were observed between triploids and tetraploids. Diploid advertisement calls have spectral and temporal properties that significantly differ from those of both triploid and tetraploid advertisement calls. Diploids produce significantly longer calls with higher pulse-rates and lower frequencies than those of tetraploids. Although strong associations are found between some temporal and spectral call parameters and body size of the calling male, our analyses demonstrate that the observed differences in advertisement calls cannot be explained as the by-product of body size differentiation only. We address the question of the factors that could be responsible for these differences: whether they are a direct consequence of poliploidy or, whether they should be seen as the result of an evolutionary process of diversification.

title: Testing morphometric theories on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses: examples from characid and atherinopsid fishes

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, Field Museum, Roosevelt Rd. at Lakeshore Drive, Chicago, IL 60605 USA

abstract_text: The diversity of sizes and shapes within and among groups of fishes is one of the principal features of their evolutionary history. To understand as much as possible about the history of size and shape evolution, two important components must be explored: phylogeny and environment. The evolution of size and shape have often been discussed in the context of developmental theories involving differential growth (allometry), differential timing (heterochrony), developmental integration, etc. The purpose of this presentation will be to examine ways in which developmental theories of size and shape diversity are tested on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses. The data comprise ontogenetic series of landmarks from clades of characid (Bryconops) and atherinopsid (Atherinella) fishes, fit to a reference form, from which the relative warps and relative-warp scores are calculated. Phylogenetic and environmental components of form change among species within clades is analyzed from both partial least squares confirmatory factor analyses. The results show that in contrast to expectations derived from the literature, large amounts of the variance in form-change among species are explained by phylogenetic hypotheses of species relationships.

title: Reduction of the dorsal spine in some Ethiopian populations of East African small barb (Barbus paludinosus): parallel microevolutionary changes or speciation?

authors.affiliation: Severtsov Institute of Ecology and Evolution, Moscow 117071, Russia
Severtsov Institute of Ecology and Evolution, Moscow 117071, Russia
Museum of Natural History, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, 66045, U.S.A.
