abstract_text: Barbus paludinosus, a diploid, small African barb species is widely distributed from South Africa to the Horn of Africa. It was previously reported from the Ethiopian Rift Valley and the closely related species, B. humilis, was reported from Lake Tana. We found B. paludinosus in the upper reaches of the White Nile, Blue Nile, and Omo River drainages. This species normally has a strong serrated spine in the dorsal fin. At two localities in the upper reaches of the White Nile and Omo tributaries, populations are characterized by a greatly reduced dorsal spine. In the same drainages, barbs with the normal dorsal spine morphology occur about 20 km downstream. The borderline between forms with normal and reduced dorsal spine morphology apparently coincides with the upper limit of distribution of the hexaploid large barb species, the only potential predator in the naturally depauperated fish communities inhabiting the upper reaches of the both river drainages. The distance between locations where the form with reduced dorsal spine occurs is more than 200 km. These locations are separated by the drainage system of a large tributary of the Blue Nile, where only the normal form was found. The morphological description of the Ethiopian populations of B. paludinosus with and without dorsal spine is presented. In order to test hypothesis about independent reduction of the dorsal spine in barbs from the two distant locations the karyological and mtDNA comparisons were made.

title: Morphological differentiation between populations of the frecklebelly madtom, Noturus munitus (Teleostei: Ictaluridae)

authors.affiliation: Biodiversity and Systematics, Box 870345, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487-0345 USA
Biodiversity and Systematics, Box 870345, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487-0345 USA
Biodiversity and Systematics, Box 870345, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487-0345 USA

abstract_text: The upper Coosa River basin poses a particularly perplexing biogeographic problem; it harbors isolated populations of many species of fishes otherwise found below the Fall Line. Over 17 species exhibit this distributional pattern to some degree. The already recognized high degree of endemism in the drainage (Percina antesella, P. jenkinsi, Etheostoma etowahae, E. scotti, etc.) suggests the possibility of cryptic species in other, more 'widespread' taxa. We examined morphometric and meristic variation across the range of the frecklebelly madtom, Noturus munitus. The populations in the Etowah and Conasauga Rivers possess a unique suite of morphological characters, including differences in shape and pigmentation, when compared with populations from the Pearl, Cahaba, and Tombigbee Rivers. We are in the process of analyzing genetic variation within this species and other closely related members of Rabida to identify phylogenetic relationships within this complex. Conservation and biogeographic implications will be discussed.

title: Did vicariance mold phenotypes of cyprinid fishes in western North America? Evidence from the Gila River basin of Arizona

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology and Museum, Arizona State University, Tempe AZ 85287-1501 USA
Department of Biology and Museum, Arizona State University, Tempe AZ 85287-1501 USA
Oklahoma Biological Survey, University of Oklahoma, Norman OK 73019 USA

abstract_text: Patterns of morphological variation in a group of western North American cyprinid fishes (the 'Gila robusta' complex of the Gila River basin of Arizona and New Mexico) has long puzzled fish taxonomists. Three different forms, (G. robusta, G. intermedia, and G. nigra) are recognized, yet their basin-wide distributions are a disjunct mosaic. Several hypotheses have been offered to accommodate this aberrant pattern: ecotypy/ecophenotypy (i.e., individual or populational response to local conditions), hybridization/intergradation (i.e., gene flow between differentiated species or races); and vicariance (an historical explanation related to regional hydrographic evolution). To represent these hypotheses, 33 sample locations were scored within the basin with regard to stream size, stream elevation, stream barriers, and paleodrainage pattern (the latter accomplished by superimposing sites onto maps depicting drainage patterns during six different geologic epochs). Morphometric data, collected from 25 individuals at all 33 sites, were then contrasted against the 9 test matrices using two- and three-way Mantel tests. A vicariance model was the only hypothesis proficient in explaining extant diversity of fish phenotypes. Of those reconstructions used in this model, only the Pliocene epoch was significantly associated with extant distributions of phenotypes.

title: Coevolutionary hypotheses and evolution of mate discrimination in a gynogenetic species complex of Amazon mollies

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin, TX 78712 USA

abstract_text: Gynogenetic female Amazon mollies (Poecilia formosa) mate with sexual males (P. latipinna) for successful reproduction. Studies show that males distinguish between conspecific females and gynogens, and preferentially mate with the former. However, the existence of gynogens indicates mate discrimination is imperfect. The Red Queen Hypothesis has been applied to this system suggesting the evolution of mate recognition is a coevolutionary 'arms race'; the lack of genetic contribution by males to gynogenetic offspring imposes selection for male discrimination that favors sexual females. This, in turn, imposes selection on gynogens to evolve characters that override male discrimination. This assumes gynogenetic females have evolved since their origination. Amazons originated with a hybridization between P. mexicana and P. latipinna at least several thousand years ago. If a coevolutionary hypothesis is true, extant gynogens should differ from ancestral gynogens. In this study first generation sexual hybrids were used as an analog for the ancestral gynogens to test this hypothesis. The predictions are gynogens will have an enhanced ability to attract sexual males, males will prefer gynogens over hybrids, and females will differ in agonistic behavior. The results of this study do not support these predictions. This suggests application of such hypotheses to gynogenetic systems be preceded by studies documenting the presence of evolutionary change in the species of interest.

title: Evolutionary relationships of the species of the genus Paralabrax (Serranidae, Perciformes) based on morphological and molecular data

authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Section of Vertebrates (Ichthyology), 900 Exposition Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90007 USA

abstract_text: The sandbasses of the genus Paralabrax are New World fishes from the Eastern Pacific and Western Atlantic. Because the sister group relationships of the Serranin genera related to Paralabrax were unknown, they were resolved first. Osteological characters of the cranium and pelvic girdle support the monophyly of Cratinus-Paralabrax-Centropristis. The nine species of Paralabrax share derived features of urohyal configuration, pterygiophore structure in dorsal and anal fins, and structure of lateral line scales. A cladistic analysis based on morphological and molecular (cytochrome b gene) data suggests an early separation of two groups. One is predominantly South American and includes 5 species: dewegeri from the Atlantic (Venezuela-Brazil), humeralis (Chile-Peru), callaensis (Ecuador), and albomaculatus (Galapagos). Interestingly, the species clathratus belongs to this group but is found in the Northeastern Pacific. The other group is composed of 4 Northern hemisphere species: loro (Central America-Baja California), auroguttatus, maculatofasciatus and nebulifer (which are predominantly found from Baja to Central California). A hypothesis of relationships is presented. The species of Paralabrax seem to have evolved recently, in the last 4-10 million years, in contrast with the species of Centropristis, which appear to be significantly older.

title: Comparative biogeography of two species of poeciliid fishes from Mexico

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, New York University, Washington Square, NY 10003, USA
Department of Biology, New York University, Washington Square, NY 10003, USA

abstract_text: Patterns of geographical variation in AP-PCR (RAPD) markers were compared between two species of Poeciliid fishes. Thirty-one populations of the variable platyfish Xiphophorus variatus and thirteen populations of the killifish Heterandria jonesi were studied. These species overlap in range in central-eastern Mexico, in freshwaters from the Rio Tamesi drainage, south to the Rio Nautla. Six primers revealed 266 scoreable bands in X. variatus and 189 in H. jonesi (163 and 124 informative characters, respectively). Parsimony analysis of the data was performed in X. variatus by heuristic search for the shortest cladograms. The data for H. jonesi are still being gathered, and a subset of only eight populations was analysed (exhaustive search). The results support three geographically disjunct clades in each species: a northern clade centered in the Tamesi drainage, a south-eastern clade in the lowlands of the Rios Cazones, Tecolutla, Solteros and Nautla, and a south-western clade, more upstream in these rivers. We hypothesize that the same geographical barriers have affected the variation in both species. Relevant geographic barriers are not obvious, however. We suggest that the south-eastern and south-western populations are divided by elevation, while the northern populations are separated from the southern populations by unsuitable habitat of slow-flowing waters. It is also worth noting that populations of X. evelynae are nested entirely within the geographic range of the south-west clade and are indistinguishable from them. This raises the question of whether it is a valid species or whether all of the fish in the south-west clade might really be X. evelynae, rather than X. variatus.

title: Diversity and distribution of the genus "Garra" (Pisces: Cyprinidae) in Africa

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Ichthyology, American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th St., New York, NY 10024 USA; City College of the City University of New York USA

abstract_text: The study aims at resolving the taxonomic jumble among the African species of the genus "Garra" and establish their present geographic distribution. Extensive field collections have been made from Ethiopian freshwater bodies where the diversity of the genus is believed to be relatively high. Available museum specimens have been investigated. Morphology and morphometries have been used to identify the species. According to preliminary results, twelve forms (species?) are recognized from Ethiopia, five of which are new. Four of the "forms" are found in six other African countries while the remaining eight are known only from Ethiopia. 'G. dembeensis' is the most abundant and widely distributed species found in 75% of the drainage basins of Ethiopia and in six other African countries. Seven other species of the genus are known to occur in ten other African countries. Generally, the genus has so far been reported from fifteen African countries. The range is from Ethiopia in the east to Guinea in the west and from Chad in the north to Tanzania in the south. The historical biogeography of the genus is controversial.

title: Female preference for trait symmetry in addition to trait size in swordtail fish

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Ohio University, Athens OH 45701 USA

abstract_text: Interest in fluctuating asymmetries, random deviations from perfect bilateral symmetry, has spread to studies of sexual selection because of the intriguing idea that females could use the degree of asymmetry of a male trait to assess the genetic quality of potential mates. The evidence that females prefer males with symmetrical sexual signals, however, has remained controversial. A problem that applies to most previous studies is that preference for trait size can be misinterpreted as preference for symmetry, even when overall trait size is held constant, if females assess trait size by the largest minimum on one side. If overall trait size is equal between males, the asymmetrical males will have the maximum and minimum trait size, and so preference to mate with symmetrical males could actually reflect a preference to avoid males with the minimum trait on one side. Xiphophorus cortezi females preferred males with symmetrical bar numbers when the minimum number of bars was held constant. The strength of female preference for the symmetrical males with fewer bars was negatively correlated with the strength of preference the same females had for bar number. These results clearly demonstrate that females preferred trait symmetry in addition to trait size.

title: Female zebrafish (Danio rerio) prefer larger males

authors.affiliation: Penn State Erie, Station Road, Erie, PA 16563 USA

abstract_text: I tested for female preferences of male body size in zebrafish (Danio rerio). My experimental design allowed females to view a small and a large male in adjacent aquaria. Time that females spent near males was scored from 20 min replays of videos. The average standard length (SL) of large males was 28 mm and small males were 22 mm. The average difference between small and large male SL in individual experiments was 6.4 mm. Females spent significantly more time near large males (average = 647 s) than small males (average = 550 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.02). When female time near males was scored only if the males were adjacent to the female, females also spent significantly more time near large males (178 s) than near small males (117 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.05). My current experiments are to test for female preference of male yellow coloration by filtering out yellow light from experimental males, and to use DNA fingerprinting to identify paternity in competitive matings.

title: Inter-population comparison of multiple paternity in the Trinidadian guppy

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Mount Allison University, Sackville, NB, E4L 1G7
Department of Biology, Mount Allison University, Sackville, NB, E4L 1G7

abstract_text: Multiple-male mating by females and the resulting sperm competition are widespread in animals. Benefits accrued by males that inseminate many females include increased reproductive success. However, the reasons underlying multiple mating by females are ambiguous since a single insemination can fertilize all her ova and mating involves potential costs to both sexes. One such cost is an increased risk of predation. Recent studies have shown that animals can assess the local risk of predation and, in response to high risk, females may decrease their mate choosiness and males may increase their use of alternative mating tactics. If predation risk increases the relative frequency of sneaky copulations in males and reduces choosiness in females, then we predict a higher frequency of concurrent multiple paternity per brood in females originating from high-predation populations as compared to females from low-predation populations. To test this hypothesis, genetic data from a polymorphic microsatellite locus was employed to conservatively estimate multiple paternity in eight populations of the Trinidadian guppy (Poecilia reticulata) differing in fish predation regime. Our data suggest that, on average, the frequency of concurrent multiple paternity is three times greater in high-predation populations than in low-predation populations. These results further suggest that predation risk reduces the variance in male mating success and thus the opportunity for sexual selection within populations.

title: Nest defense by the exotic fish, round goby (Neogobius melanostomus), on a shipwreck in western Lake Erie

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, ON N9B
Department of Biological Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, ON N9B

abstract_text: Our observations of round goby nesting behaviour on shipwrecks in the western basin of Lake Erie using a video camera indicate that these fish spawn at much greater depths (7 m) than previously reported (< 2m). Of the species that approached the exposed nest (rock bass, smallmouth bass, yellow perch, logperch, round gobies), most behavioural interactions occurred between the guarding male and other round gobies. During 12 minutes of observation, there were 63 instances in which round gobies approached the nest and in 4 cases, intruders fed on eggs. In response, the guarding male approached (34 times), chased (18 times) and hit (4 times) round goby intruders. The response by the resident goby to the presence of rock bass (1 swam by and 7 approached) resulted in 6 approaches, 4 chases and 1 hit. The resident male responded to juvenile smallmouth bass (3 swam by and 1 approached) only once by approaching the intruder. The guarding male did not respond to either logperch or yellow perch. We anticipate that recruitment of round gobies will increase substantially in Lake Erie owing to the presence of artificial reefs (shipwrecks) and the ability of guarding males to defend nests effectively.

title: Context dependent alarm behavior in the estuarine fish Fundulus heteroclitus

authors.affiliation: Duke University Marine Laboratory, 135 Duke Marine Lab Rd., Beaufort, NC 28516 USA

abstract_text: Fundulus heteroclitus live in tidal creeks where predation risk varies with the structure of the microhabitat and time of year. Structure of the microhabitat varies as a function of the tides. Accurate recognition and response to predators is essential to the survival of prey. This study investigated alarm behavior of adult and juvenile estuarine fish, F. heteroclitus. Activity was determined in response to conspecific alarm chemical in relatively deep and shallow water (aquaria and fingerbowls). In deep water, in the fall, F. heteroclitus show container dependent alarm behavior. Both adult and juvenile fish showed a significant decrease in activity in response to alarm chemical compared addition of control. However, in shallow fingerbowls neither adults or juveniles show a decrease in activity. Adults also show seasonal context dependent alarm behavior. In winter adults in aquaria show no change in activity in response to alarm chemicals. Accurate responses to alarm chemicals may be those that are modulated by context, such as water depth, that reflects the actual risk of predation. Field experiments will determine if these results extend to the field.

title: The role of choice and performance in determining the diets of juvenile sculpins

authors.affiliation: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92717 USA

abstract_text: Diet studies often measure selectivity, or the proportion of diet made up by specific prey types compared to their occurrence in the environment. This measure is the result of two events: the choice to attack that prey type and whether the attack results in a successful capture. This study quantified these two events separately in the juveniles of three species of sculpin (Cottidae) to compare their roles in determining the taxonomic composition of the diet. Choice showed a greater influence on the occurrence of harpacticoid copepods and gammarid amphipods in the diet than performance. Significant interspecific differences in choice of harpacticoids and gammarids were found to be correlated with differences in the occurrence of these prey types in the diets of the three species. Performance played a greater role in determining the occurrence of calanoid copepods in the diet than did choice. Species and individuals with high capture success on calanoids did not choose to attack this prey type more often than those with lower capture success. This study indicates that classic measures of selectivity will only reflect active choice or avoidance when capture success on a prey type is high.

title: Burrow distribution and diel behavior of Pholidichthys leucotaenia (family Pholidichthyidae) on coral reefs, Solomon Islands

authors.affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742
10600 Stoneyhill Ct., Silver Spring, MD 20901
1488 Klines Run Rd., Wrightsville, PA 17368

abstract_text: Diel behavior was studied on pairs of adults living in burrows and juveniles sharing these burrows. Juveniles retire into burrows at dusk and emerge at dawn to break into large swarms, feeding on plankton as far as 10 m from their home burrow at depths 4 to 34 m. Adults clean their burrows by spitting out sand and carrying out rubble. At night neither adults nor juveniles emerge from their burrows. Burrow entrances were observed continuously for periods of 2 to 35 hours with low light and regular video cameras. Disturbances to their burrow entrances by other fish and a large octopus caused only a temporary break in their cleaning activity. Heads of adults emerged the most (1/3 of total length) and stayed out longest (1/2 min) when they were not cleaning out their burrows but appeared to look around or lunge at other fishes. They may cannibalize their young as food. The swimming and feeding behavior of juvenile P. leucotaenia (sometimes called "mimic catfish") do not resemble that of the venomous catfish, Plotosus lineatus. Sixteen reefs were surveyed at Guadalcanal, and the Florida, Russell, and New Georgia islands. P. leucotaenia were found in all except the isolated St. Marys Island.

title: Blennies on offshore petroleum platforms: similarity of assemblage structure among platforms and the effect of a hurricane

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biological Sciences, The University of Southern Mississippi, Box 5018, Hattiesburg, MS 30406-5018 USA

abstract_text: Marine fish assemblages may be viewed as being structured by deterministic or chaotic processes. To understand factors important in structuring an assemblage of four blenniid species (Family: Blenniidae) I collected data on their abundance and distribution in early July 1997 on six offshore petroleum platforms. Hurricane Danny passed through the study area 50 km offshore of the Louisiana coast in mid July. Between late August and mid-September I collected data on nine platforms in the same area. I conducted visual censuses on diagonal cross-members of the platforms at depths of 1, 5, 10, and 15 m. Blennies displayed a distinct vertical zonation with Scartella cristata confined to the upper 2 m and Parablennius marmoreus limited to 10-15 m depths. I used Morisita's index (Im) to investigate blenniid assemblage similarity among platforms and the effect of the hurricane. Im values were compared to a null model of randomly generated data. Platforms were similar in assemblage structure with three of the four depths sampled having average Im's > 1. Pre- and post-hurricane Im's averaged greater than one in three of the four depths sampled, indicating that this disturbance did not affect these blenniid assemblages.

title: FAD-associated fishes: factors affecting aggregation size and composition

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011-5640

abstract_text: I studied near-shore, juvenile reef fishes associated with floating objects along the Pacific coast of Panama. Using naturally-occurring flotsam and Fish Aggregation Devices (FADs), I made observations and conducted experiments on factors affecting group size and species composition. Increased FAD size and the presence of fouling biota positively affected aggregation sizes and the number of fish species present. FADs hung with model fish, lead weights and unmanipulated control FADs did not differ significantly in aggregation size or composition. However, drifting FADs deployed with live fish (Abudefduf troschelii) appeared to recruit additional fish more than those deployed without fish. The species composition of aggregations associated with drifting flotsam differed from aggregations found with anchored flotsam and anchored FADs. At an array of anchored FADs, species composition was predictable over days to weeks, but showed distinct changes over a period of months.

title: Pikes and muskies: mudminnows gone bad?

authors.affiliation: University of Washington Fish Collection, Box 355100, Seattle, WA 98195, USA

abstract_text: The phylogenetic intra-relationships of esocoid fishes have been examined repeatedly in systematic studies with contradictory results. The pre-Tertiary origin of the group and low Recent diversity likely contribute to the apparent paucity of apomorphic characters that define esocoid clades. Currently, the Esocoidei contains two families, the Esocidae and Umbridae, with Esox coextensive with Esocidae, and Dallia, Novumbra, and Umbra comprising the Umbridae. Generally, the following inter-generic relationships are accepted: (Esox (Novumbra (Dallia, Umbra))), but the literature abounds with conflicting evidence. Phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequence data from the 16S rRNA and cytochrome b mitochondrial genes strongly support a previously overlooked hypothesis of esocoid relationships. Parsimony and maximum likelihood analyses show a paraphyletic Umbridae in the following set of esocoid relationships: (Umbra (Dallia (Novumbra, Esox))). Published studies of esocoid karyotypes, allozymes, and fossils offer supporting evidence for the DNA-derived hypothesis. A survey of published data on esocoid anatomy may reveal previously unrecognized morphological synapomorphies to diagnose the newly postulated clades.

title: The phylogenetic systematics of the Goodeidae (Cyprinodontiformes)

authors.affiliation: Division of Fishes - UMMZ, University of Michigan, 1109 Geddes Ave., Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1079 USA

abstract_text: Goodeine fishes are remarkable for the degree to which they provision developing embryos. A suite of physiological and morphological traits permits internal fertilization, pronounced matrotrophy, and live birth in this natural group from the central plateau of Mexico. Morphological and nucleic acid sequence (COI) data form the basis of a phylogenetic analysis of goodeid interrelationships. Forty-one species from 18 genera comprise the ingroup, and members of the Cyprinodontidae, Fundulidae, Poeciliidae, Profundulidae, and Oxyzygonectes are utilized as outgroups to polarize character states. Monophyly of the Goodeidae, and the sister-group relationship of the Goodeinae and Empetrichthyinae, is supported. The Profundulidae is supported as the sister-group to the Goodeidae. Early diversification events within the Goodeinae are not well supported, potentially indicating rapid radiation of the major lineages. The evolution and biogeography of the Goodeidae will be discussed.

title: Morphological diversification and developmental variation in a Bahamian pupfish species complex

authors.affiliation: Corson Hall, Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-2701 USA

abstract_text: Variation in trophic morphology is widespread in teleosts. The sources of this variation have been explored in a number of studies, and the genetic and environmental basis for extreme variation have been identified in a variety of fish. Here, I address the role development plays in producing phenotypic variation in a putative species complex of the Bahamian pupfish Cyprinodon. This taxon offers an excellent opportunity to address the origin of morphological variation in closely related species, because sympatrically occurring Cyprinodon exhibit a striking diversity in feeding morphology and behavior, yet putative species show only partial reproductive isolation. Offspring from three species and their hybrids were bred in the lab, and ontogenetic trajectories of their feeding morphology were followed until maturity. In Cyprinodon, very small differences in growth rates translate into large differences in feeding morphology. This developmental program has implications for large-scale, macroevolutionary patterns.

title: Revision of the South American shovelnose catfishes of the genus Sorubim (Siluriformes: Pimelodidae), with a description of two new species

authors.affiliation: Southern Illinois University, Dept. of Zoology, Carbondale, IL 62901-6501

abstract_text: The systematics and taxonomic history of the genus Sorubim (Teleostei: Pimelodidae) is unclear because of confusing and inadequate descriptive taxonomic literature. To assess the taxonomic status of species in the genus, I examined 347 specimens for morphological variation, including analysis of morphometry, meristics, osteology, and pigmentation throughout the known geographic range. An extensive literature review of the ten named species allocated to Sorubim and analysis of morphological data support the recognition of four species: Sorubim lima, widespread in the Amazon, Parana, and Orinoco basins; S. elongatus n. sp., occurring in the Essequibo, Orinoco, and upper Amazon drainages; S. caudacuspis n. sp., endemic to the Rio Magdalena and Lago Maracaibo drainages in Northwestern South America; and S. trigonocephalus, known only from the Rio Tapajos region in Brazil. The taxonomic revision presented includes a redescription of the genus, recognition of two nominal species as valid, descriptions of two new species, a dichotomous key, and distributional data for all nominal forms. Because of the small sample sizes available for S. trigonocephalus, future study of this species is warranted. All species of Sorubim are significant components of the ornamental fish trade and frequently found in local markets as a source of subsistence protein.

title: Phylogenetic relationships of the superfamily Poecilioidea (Cyprinodontiformes: Teleostei) as inferred from morphological data

authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045-2454 USA

abstract_text: The superfamily Poecilioidea contains approximately 300 species of fishes in two families, the Anablepidae (13 spp.) and the Poeciliidae (approx. 287 spp.). The monophyly of this superfamily has been supported by previous studies using morphology and DNA sequence data. However, the phylogenetic relationships within the group have been controversial. This phylogenetic analysis of over 90 transformation series and 30 representative poecilioid species supports the monophyly of the two included families. The poeciliine tribes Heterandrini, Poeciliini, and Cnesterodontini as traditionally recognized are shown to be nonmonophyletic. The facultatively viviparous species Tomeurus gracilis is nested within the poeciliine tribe Cnesterodontini and represents an evolutionary loss of obligate viviparity. Based on the phylogeny, the genus Aplocheilichthys should be restricted to the type species, Aplocheilichthys spilauchen, and Micropanchax should be recognized as the valid genus for most of the species previously placed in Aplocheilichthys. The evolution of viviparity and pelagic lacustrine habits in this group will be discussed.

title: Phylogenetic systematics of snubnose darters (Percidae) and the evolution of male breeding color

authors.affiliation: Illinois Natural History Survey, 607 East Peabody Drive, Champaign, IL 61820, USA

abstract_text: Snubnose darters are a fascinating group of fishes in the genus Etheostoma; breeding males exhibit some of the most fantastic colors found in North American fishes. The results of an analysis of complete cytochrome b DNA sequences (1140 base pairs) for 32 species of snubnose darters and putative close relatives are presented. Topologies obtained with parsimony, distance, and maximum likelihood criteria are congruent. The phylogenetic hypothesis supports relationships within snubnose darters that are corroborated with other evidence, although it differs from previous hypotheses in basal relationships. The cytochrome b gene tree suggests that snubnose darters are polyphyletic, with members of the subgenus Etheostoma s.s. related to one clade, and that members of the E. variatum species group are not closely related to snubnose darters or to Etheostoma s.s. The phylogeny is used for studying the evolution of several male breeding color characters that were coded and mapped onto the tree, and sexual selection experiments determined that these breeding colors were important to male reproductive success. This combination of evidence is used to propose a role for sexual selection in the differentiation of snubnose darter lineages and species.

title: Molecular phylogeny of the gobioid fishes

authors.affiliation: Museum of Zoology, Division of Fishes, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109 USA

abstract_text: The perciform suborder Gobioidei contains an estimated 2000 species in 270 genera, found throughout the world oceans and freshwaters. This lineage is very diverse and reductive evolution is common, making traditional morphological systematic studies particularly difficult. In an attempt to resolve relationships among gobioid groups, I sequenced a 2022 base pair fragment of the mitochondrial genome, comprising the entire ND1 and ND2 genes for 40 gobioid species and performed phylogenetic analysis using cladistic parsimony methods. My data set includes representatives of the Gobiidae (including all subfamilies: Gobiinae, Gobionellinae, Oxudercinae, Amblyopinae and Sicydiinae), Microdesmidae (both subfamilies: Microdesminae and Ptereleotrinae), Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae; representatives of the Eleotrididae were used as outgroup taxa. Analysis of the nucleotide data yielded a single phylogeny for which Bremer support and jackknife indices indicated weaker support in the deeper nodes. Analysis of translated amino acid data yielded two phylogenies differing only in the placement of one taxon; this phylogeny is congruent in many respects with gobioid relationships suggested by morphological characters. My analysis provides a broad view of gobioid relationships and, in particular, provides evidence for the relationships of the paedomorphic Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae within the Gobioidei.

title: A phylogenetic study of the neotropical hypopomid electric fishes (Rhamphichthyoidea: Gymnotiformes)

authors.affiliation: Cornell University, Division of Biological Sciences, Section of Neurobiology and Behavior, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA

abstract_text: The monophyly of the rhamphichthyoid gymnotiforms is supported by previous phylogenetic studies of gymnotiform fishes. In contrast, the status and relationships of the constituent subgroups of the rhamphichthyoids remain poorly understood. The goal of this work was to determine whether the currently recognized rhamphichthyoid taxa represent monophyletic groups and to ascertain the species-level relationships among them, with special emphasis on the Family Hypopomidae Mago-Leccia, 1976. An additional goal was to gain insight into the evolution of the species-specific electric organ discharge (EOD). A phylogenetic study of 23 rhamphichthyoid species was carried out based on mitochondrial DNA sequence data from the portions of the 12S rRNA, 16S rRNA and cytochrome b genes and a morphological data set. Results indicate that nominal hypopomid genera Steatogenys and Hypopygus do not form a clade with other nominal hypopomids but strongly support the monophyly of the remaining nominal hypopomids. Additionally, the nominal species of Brachyhypopomus form a clade with five new species. Genus Brachyhypopomus is the sister taxon to the monotypic genus Microstemarchus which together form the sister group to genus Hypopomus. Complex EODs and a monophasic EOD appear to have arisen within the Hypopomidae independently of these character states in outgroup taxa.

title: A preliminary phylogenetic analysis of the subfamily Amphiprioninae (Perciformes: Pomacentridae)

authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045-2454 USA

abstract_text: The Amphiprioninae is a subfamily of marine fishes, commonly called anemonefishes, composed of two genera (Amphiprion and Premnas) with approximately 28 species. The phylogenetic relationships within this subfamily are poorly understood. Although a hypothetical set of relationships has been previously proposed, the phylogeny of the group has never been fully examined. Previous work has suggested that the members of this subfamily are divided among six species complexes. At least one representative species from all six of these complexes and three outgroup (pomacentrid) genera were examined. Morphological characters, primarily osteological ones, were used to conduct a phylogenetic analysis of this subfamily. The preliminary results will be presented and evolution of the fish-anemone relationship will be discussed.

title: Speciation studies in the Percina subgenus Swainia (Percidae: Etheostomatinae)

authors.affiliation: Illinois Natural History Survey

abstract_text: Hypotheses concerning modes of allopatric speciation make explicit predictions regarding patterns of phylogenetic and biogeographic diversification. This investigation will test allopatric speciation models using phylogenetic and biogeographic information for the subgenus Swainia, a monophyletic group of four described species in the genus Percina. Complete gene sequences of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b have been collected from all species of Swainia, including individuals from multiple populations of P. phoxocephala and P. nasuta. Patterns of nucleotide variation were investigated and phylogenetic relationships were estimated using maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood, and distance optimality criteria. Heterogeneity of nucleotide substitution rate was examined using both maximum parsimony relative rate tests and a likelihood ratio test. Inferred phylogenetic relationships, biogeographic patterns, and relative amounts of nucleotide divergence are used to develop hypotheses of speciation in Swainia.

title: Biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes: patterns of faunal occurrence in southeastern Australia

authors.affiliation: Biology Department, Arizona State University, Tempe AZ 85287-1501, USA

abstract_text: This presentation is part of a wider study of the biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes. Southeastern Australia is hereby defined as coastal drainages from the Fitzroy River through Gulf of St. Vincent, including the inland Murray system separated from coastal drainages by the Great Dividing Range. It has the following biogeographic relationships of fishes restricted to freshwater: 1) 5 of 8 species from southern Victoria also occur in the Murray system; and 2) 18 of 27 species (or species pairs) co-occur between coastal Queensland drainages and the Murray system. The relationships of an additional 6 species endemic to the Murray system are more obscure. Biogeographic connectivity between the Murray and surrounding drainages thus appears high. Past biogeographic explanations for these relationships have relied heavily upon river captures, making faunal distributions easily explained. However, the last 15 years have seen a paradigm shift in the proposed evolution of the Great Dividing Range including evidence that river captures are either non-existent or very old (> 30-60 mya). Most patterns are congruent with present geological scenarios although exceptions exist. The new geologic conclusions are assessed on the basis of biological evidence and new hypotheses are provided to explain present distribution patterns.

title: Phylogenetic relationships and biogeography of the malagasy cichlidae

authors.affiliation: Museum of Zoology, Fish Division, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1079 USA

abstract_text: Phylogenetic relationships of the endemic Malagasy cichlids were investigated using DNA sequence data and combined evidence. Prior attempts based on morphological evidence to generate a highly supported and resolved phylogenetic hypothesis have been only partially successful, and this lack of resolution has been attributed to muted anatomical variation and a high degree of convergence/parallelism within Cichlidae. DNA sequence data is presented corresponding to two regions of the mitochondrial genome for a representative sampling of cichlid taxa, including all of the known Malagasy cichlids. The use of molecular sequence data results in a highly resolved phylogenetic hypothesis for Cichlidae. However, support for higher-level relationships is relatively weak, and may indicate that differentiation in ancient cichlid lineages occurred over a relatively short time. Results based on DNA sequence data indicate that the Malagasy cichlids (including the Asian genera) are not monophyletic, that the Etropline cichlids (Etroplus from India/Sri Lanka and Paretroplus from Madagascar) form a natural group, and that the Ptychochromine cichlids (including Oxylapia) are a monophyletic Malagasy assemblage. Biogeography of the Malagasy cichlids, and Cichlidae in general, will also be discussed.

title: An amphibian survey at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas
abstract_text: An amphibian survey was initiated at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas to assess anecdotal observations of anuran population declines. From February to July 1997, 12 amphibian species were documented at the park. Sixty-nine sites used by amphibians were identified, of which 73% contained evidence of breeding. It does not appear that amphibian species are in decline at Brazos Bend State Park. In February 1998, 350 meters of PVC pipe were installed at selected sites to evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in regard to hylid frog populations. These and other sites are currently being monitored in order to gain insight to amphibian population dynamics at Brazos Bend State Park.

title: Amphibian species distribution patterns in an agriculturally-fragmented landscape

authors.affiliation: Dept. Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907-1159, USA
Dept. Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907-1159, USA

abstract_text: Apparent declines of amphibian populations in many parts of the world have caused great concern in recent years. This study was conducted to determine what effects agriculturally induced fragmentation of forests has had on amphibian assemblages and their distribution in a midwestern landscape. Potential breeding pools and upland areas in 30 forest patches of various sizes and degrees of isolation were intensively sampled for amphibians from April through August 1996 and March through August 1997. Species presence was documented by using pitfall trapping, anuran vocalization surveys, cover board sampling, minnow traps, and dipnetting for larva. Amphibian, anuran and salamander assemblages were all nonrandomly distributed across the landscape. Bufo americanus and Hyla versicolor were ubiquitous whereas the distribution of several species including Ambystoma tigrinum, A. texanum, Plethodon cinereus, Rana clamitans, and R. pipiens showed significant nesting. Overall, species richness was significantly associated with a weighted measure of wetland permanency (WETWGT, p=0.0001, WETWGTC2, p=0.0029), with forest patches which have seasonal and semi-permanent wetlands containing more species. Abundance of amphibians was significantly associated with forest proximity (LOGPR, p=0.0001, LOGPRC2, p=0.0037), with more isolated patches having greater amphibian abundance. The observed distribution and degree of nestedness exhibited by several amphibians suggests that these species respond to landscape-level factors.

title: Response of the herpetofaunal community to three sandhill restoration treatments on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida

authors.affiliation: Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, University of Florida, Box 110430, Gainesville, FL 32611-430

abstract_text: The longleaf pine ecosystem, once widespread in the southeastern United States, has been reduced by as much as 98%. Restoration of this endangered ecosystem can be a mechanism for conservation, in an attempt to reverse existing damage and create more resilient communities. Restoration methods implemented in sandhills must be based in a deep knowledge of the ecosystem to effectively recreate and manage all aspects. Consequently, restoration success can only be evaluated by examining community response. Since reptiles and amphibians occupy the ecosystem at a fairly small scale, these communities may be important indicators of microhabitat restoration success. Previous work on herpetofaunal response to disturbance regimes has demonstrated the complexity of the effects and the importance of habitat structure. Habitat requirements for sandhill herpetofauna are very diverse, demonstrating the need to closely examine these communities when making management decisions. My study, focused on reptiles and amphibians, is one portion of a multi-agency investigation of three sandhill restoration techniques on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida: fire, oak-specific herbicide, and mechanical oak felling. Pitfall traps and drift fences were used to capture reptiles and amphibians in restoration treatment areas, control plots and 'typical' longleaf pine sandhill areas during the summer of 1997. Animals were identified to species, marked, sexed, weighed, measured, and visually examined. Vegetative cover data were also collected. The objective of this project is to examine herpetofaunal species richness and abundance, as well as population age class structure and sex ratios, with regards to the restoration treatment and vegetative structure.

title: Anuran assemblages in anthropogenically and pyrogenically disturbed landscapes of the boreal forest

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Victoria, PO Box 3020 STN CSC, Victoria BC V8W 3N5, Canada

abstract_text: Alberta-Pacific Forest Industries Inc. (AL-PAC) operates a large pulp mill in the mixed-wood boreal forest of northeastern Alberta. The company harvests within its 6,000,000 ha Forest Management Area (FMA) using an 'ecosystem management' perspective. In other words, AL-PAC attempts to mimic fire, the dominant natural disturbance of the boreal forest. Five amphibian species, including two that appear to have undergone population declines, occur in the FMA. In 1997, I sampled anuran communities at 12 lakes to investigate whether each species showed the same relative abundance in logged, naturally burned, and undisturbed areas. I employed call surveys, transect sampling, egg and larval searches, and metamorph searches. Additionally, I conducted vegetation surveys on each transect to quantitatively examine differences in habitat. Preliminary results suggest that lakes with adjacent cutblocks support the highest number of amphibians; however, this may be a function of lake size, distance from active roads, or forest type. An analysis to separate these effects is underway.

title: The effects of forest-pasture edges on the herpetofauna of Fila Cruces, Costa Rica

authors.affiliation: Department of Natural Resources, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-3001, USA

abstract_text: Human activities tend to create highly fragmented landscapes, thereby exposing animal populations to edges. I am interested in the impacts of forest-pasture edges on the dynamics of frog and lizard populations. Using a paired-plot design I described the abundance and distribution of lizards (Norops spp.) and leaf-litter frogs (Eleutherodactylus spp.) in 10 forest fragments near Las Cruces, Costa Rica. The study took place from February to June 1997 and covered both dry and wet seasons. No species was definitively absent from the edge plots. Nocturnal leaf-litter frogs were generally equally abundant near forest edges and in forest interiors. The single diurnal eleutherodactylid species, however, was consistently more abundant in the forest interiors, suggesting that edge effects may be stronger during the day than at night. Anoline lizards were more abundant at the edges during the dry season but became more abundant in forest interiors during the wet season. This seasonal variation adds a new dimension to our understanding of edge effects, and carries important practical implications for future studies. The reproductive period of the lizards, which coincides with the rainy season, as well as lower rates of parasitism on anoline lizards near edges, are offered as possible explanations for the observed seasonal pattern.

title: Impacts of timber harvesting on surface activity in terrestrial salamanders

authors.affiliation: Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061-0321
Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061-0321
Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061-0321

abstract_text: Terrestrial salamanders spend the majority of their time in cool, moist refugia underground, but must surface to forage and breed. Although little is known about their surface activity patterns, abundance is usually inferred by counts of surface active salamanders on wet nights. Recently, such counts have been used to assess the impacts of timber harvesting on terrestrial salamanders. It is assumed in these studies that the percent of the population active on the surface is not altered by the treatment. We tested this assumption by conducting a mark-recapture study on harvested and control plots. We found significantly different proportions active between treatments. At one location, the harvested plot had a lower percent active than its control (Plethodon cinereus: 4.0% vs. 9.2%, p=.021; P. glutinosus: 3.8% vs. 11.7%, p=.091). At the other location, the harvested plots had a higher percent active than their controls (P. cinereus: 4.2% and 3.9% vs. 1.6% and 1.3%, p=.017). At this site, surface counts indicated there were more salamanders on the harvested plots than on the controls, but mark-recapture estimates indicated there were actually twice as many salamanders on the control plots.

title: Genetic diversity in drought-impacted populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach CA 90840-3702 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach CA 90840-3702 USA

abstract_text: Populations that experience a large reduction in effective size are expected to exhibit a bottleneck effect which will include loss of heterozygosity and loss of alleles. Populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida, in Central and Southern California were impacted by an extended drought that occurred from 1987-1992 and exhibited local population size decreases up to 85% during this period. I examined changes in genetic diversity in four populations of C. marmorata in the drought affected area by comparing microsatellite DNA allele frequencies from tissue samples collected before and after this drought period. Genotypes of five microsatellite loci were determined to assess the genetic diversity within these samples. Heterozygosity was used as a measurement of genetic diversity. Although no significant decline in heterozygosity was shown in the five loci, there was a decrease in the number of alleles present in the most severely impacted population. Since most individuals that were present in the post-drought samples were survivors of the drought, the first sign of decreased genetic diversity would be the loss of alleles. Changes in the level of genetic diversity (heterozygosity) would only be detectable in subsequent post-drought generations.
